claims.text: The initial HEA is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Controlled casting and thermomechanical processing minimize segregation and secondary-phase formation in the HEA.
High strain rates reduce overall dislocation mobility in the HEA.
Low temperatures reduce overall dislocation mobility in the HEA.
Reduced dislocation mobility causes localized dislocation pile-ups.
Demanding loading conditions cause or accentuate nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
Localized dislocation pile-ups act as crack-nucleation sites.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations act as crack-nucleation sites.
Inherent lattice distortion in the HEA slows dislocation motion under high-strain-rate or low-temperature loading.
Localized dislocation accumulation and compositional fluctuations produce stress concentrations that favor brittle cleavage over ductile slip.
Favoring cleavage over energy-dissipating dislocation slip reduces toughness.
At room temperature and an ambient strain rate, the HEA has ductile, high-toughness behavior with substantial plastic deformation.
Increasing strain rate from approximately 10^-3 s^-1 to approximately 10^-1 s^-1 will lower toughness relative to the ambient baseline.
Testing near 77 K will lower toughness relative to the room-temperature baseline.
High-strain-rate or low-temperature testing will reduce elongation relative to the baseline.
High-strain-rate or low-temperature testing will increase cleavage facets and reduce dimple-dominated fracture relative to the baseline.
A strain rate around 10^-1 s^-1 and temperatures down to 77 K define service conditions under which a ductile-to-brittle transition may become relevant.
The transition thresholds may depend on processing history, grain size, and local compositional variation.
